# The geometric Mahler conjectures

## Status of the problem

The two statements requested are the general and symmetric Mahler conjectures. The full conjectures for all dimensions are not proved in this manuscript. What is rigorously proved below is that the conjectured lower bounds are attained by the proposed extremizers: simplices in Part A and cubes in Part B. The general lower bounds and the full equality characterizations are not resolved here.

---

## 1. Preliminaries

Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex body. For \(z\in\operatorname{int}K\), the polar of \(K-z\) is
\[
(K-z)^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,x-z\rangle\le 1\text{ for all }x\in K\}.
\]
The volume product is
\[
P(K)=\inf_{z\in\operatorname{int}K}|K|\,|(K-z)^\circ|.
\]
The infimum is attained at the unique Santaló point.

We use the following standard affine invariance.

### Lemma 1 (affine invariance of the volume product)

If \(T(x)=Ax+b\) is an invertible affine map on \(\mathbb R^n\), then
\[
P(TK)=P(K).
\]

**Proof.** We have \(|TK|=|\det A|\,|K|\). For \(z\in\operatorname{int}K\),
\[
(TK-Tz)^\circ=(A(K-z))^\circ=A^{-T}(K-z)^\circ.
\]
Hence
\[
|(TK-Tz)^\circ|=|\det A|^{-1}|(K-z)^\circ|.
\]
Multiplying by \(|TK|\) gives the same product as for \(K\). Taking infima gives \(P(TK)=P(K)\). ∎

We also use the fact that the Santaló point is unique and is covariant under affine maps: if \(T\) is an invertible affine map, then the Santaló point of \(TK\) is \(T s(K)\).

---

## 2. Part A: simplices attain the conjectured lower bound

Let
\[
\Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\le 1\}.
\]
Then \(\Delta_n\) is a simplex, and
\[
|\Delta_n|=\frac1{n!}.
\]

Its centroid is
\[
c=\frac1{n+1}(1,\dots,1).
\]
The affine automorphism group of a simplex permutes its \(n+1\) vertices. The unique point fixed by all such automorphisms is the centroid. Since the Santaló point is unique and must be fixed by every affine automorphism of the body, the Santaló point of \(\Delta_n\) is exactly \(c\).

For \(y\in\mathbb R^n\), set
\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.
\]
For \(x\in\Delta_n\),
\[
\langle y,x\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i x_i.
\]
Since \(x_i\ge 0\) and \(\sum x_i\le 1\),
\[
\max_{x\in\Delta_n}\langle y,x\rangle=\max(0,y_1,\dots,y_n).
\]
Thus
\[
y\in(\Delta_n-c)^\circ
\]
if and only if
\[
\max(0,y_1,\dots,y_n)\le 1+\frac{S}{n+1}.
\]
This condition is equivalent to
\[
S\ge -(n+1)
\]
and, for every \(i=1,\dots,n\),
\[
y_i\le 1+\frac{S}{n+1}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(\Delta_n-c)^\circ
=
\left\{
y\in\mathbb R^n:
-S\le n+1,
\quad
(n+1)y_i-S\le n+1\ (i=1,\dots,n)
\right\}.
\]

The vertices of this polytope are
\[
v_0=(n+1,\dots,n+1)
\]
and
\[
v_k=-(n+1)e_k,\qquad k=1,\dots,n.
\]
Indeed, \(v_0\) is the intersection of the \(n\) hyperplanes
\[
(n+1)y_i-S=n+1,
\]
and each \(v_k\) is the intersection of \(-S=n+1\) with the \(n-1\) hyperplanes
\[
(n+1)y_i-S=n+1,\qquad i\ne k.
\]
Therefore
\[
(\Delta_n-c)^\circ=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,v_1,\dots,v_n\}.
\]

We compute its volume. The difference vectors are
\[
v_k-v_0=-(n+1)(e_k+\mathbf 1),
\]
where \(\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)\). The matrix with columns \(e_k+\mathbf 1\) is
\[
I+\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T,
\]
whose determinant is
\[
\det(I+\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T)=1+\mathbf 1^T\mathbf 1=n+1.
\]
Hence
\[
|\det(v_1-v_0,\dots,v_n-v_0)|=(n+1)^n(n+1)=(n+1)^{n+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
|(\Delta_n-c)^\circ|=\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{n!}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
P(\Delta_n)
=
|\Delta_n|\,|(\Delta_n-c)^\circ|
=
\frac1{n!}\cdot\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{n!}
=
\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}.
\]
Since every simplex is an affine image of \(\Delta_n\), Lemma 1 shows that every simplex attains the conjectured value.

Thus the “if” direction of the equality case in Part A is proved: every simplex satisfies
\[
P(K)=\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}.
\]
The lower bound for arbitrary \(K\), and the converse that equality occurs only for simplices, are not proved in this manuscript.

---

## 3. Part B: cubes attain the symmetric conjectured lower bound

Let
\[
K=[-1,1]^n.
\]
Then \(K=-K\), and since \(K\) is centrally symmetric, its Santaló point is \(0\). Indeed, if \(s\) is the Santaló point, then by central symmetry \(-s\) is also a Santaló point; uniqueness forces \(s=0\).

Clearly
\[
|K|=2^n.
\]
Its polar is
\[
K^\circ
=
\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle x,y\rangle\le 1\text{ for all }x\in[-1,1]^n\}
=
\left\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i|\le 1\right\}.
\]
The volume of the \(\ell_1\)-unit ball is
\[
\frac{2^n}{n!}.
\]
Indeed, the ball is partitioned into \(2^n\) orthants, and in each orthant the set is
\[
\{u_i\ge 0:\ u_1+\cdots+u_n\le 1\},
\]
which is an affine image of \(\Delta_n\) and has volume \(1/n!\).

Therefore
\[
|K|\,|K^\circ|
=
2^n\cdot \frac{2^n}{n!}
=
\frac{4^n}{n!}.
\]
So the cube attains the conjectured symmetric lower bound.

The general lower bound
\[
|K|\,|K^\circ|\ge \frac{4^n}{n!}
\]
for every centrally symmetric \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), \(n\ge 4\), and the full determination of equality cases, are not proved in this manuscript.

---

## 4. Separation of proved and unproved statements

### Proved rigorously here

- Every simplex attains
  \[
  P(K)=\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}.
  \]
- The cube \([-1,1]^n\) attains
  \[
  |K|\,|K^\circ|=\frac{4^n}{n!}.
  \]

### Not proved here

- The general Mahler lower bound
  \[
  P(K)\ge\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}
  \]
  for every convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), \(n\ge 2\).
- The equality characterization for the general Mahler conjecture beyond the fact that simplices attain the bound.
- The symmetric Mahler lower bound
  \[
  |K|\,|K^\circ|\ge\frac{4^n}{n!}
  \]
  for all centrally symmetric convex bodies in dimensions \(n\ge 4\).
- The equality cases in the symmetric Mahler conjecture beyond the cube.

Thus a complete resolution of the stated conjectures is not obtained.

# The geometric Mahler conjectures: verification of the proposed extremizers

## Final claim

This manuscript proves rigorously only the following two partial results.

1. For every simplex \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), the conjectured general Mahler value is attained:
\[
P(K)=\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}.
\]

2. The cube \([-1,1]^n\) attains the conjectured symmetric Mahler value:
\[
|[-1,1]^n|\,|([-1,1]^n)^\circ|=\frac{4^n}{n!}.
\]

The general lower bounds and the full equality characterizations of the Mahler conjectures are not proved here. No counterexample is given. Thus the stated conjectures remain unresolved in this manuscript.

---

## 1. Definitions and affine invariance

Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex body. For \(z\in\operatorname{int}K\), write
\[
(K-z)^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,x-z\rangle\le 1\text{ for every }x\in K\}.
\]
The volume product of \(K\) at \(z\) is
\[
|K|\,|(K-z)^\circ|.
\]
The Santaló point is the unique point \(s(K)\in\operatorname{int}K\) at which the volume product is minimized.

We use the following standard affine invariance.

### Lemma 1

Let \(T(x)=Ax+b\) with \(A\in GL_n(\mathbb R)\). Then for every convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\),
\[
P(TK)=P(K).
\]
More precisely, for every \(z\in\operatorname{int}K\),
\[
|TK|\,|(TK-Tz)^\circ|
=
|K|\,|(K-z)^\circ|.
\]

### Proof

Since \(TK-Tz=A(K-z)\), we have
\[
(TK-Tz)^\circ=(A(K-z))^\circ.
\]
For \(y\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
y\in (A(K-z))^\circ
\]
iff for every \(u\in K-z\),
\[
\langle y,Au\rangle\le 1,
\]
iff for every \(u\in K-z\),
\[
\langle A^T y,u\rangle\le 1,
\]
iff
\[
A^T y\in (K-z)^\circ.
\]
Thus
\[
(A(K-z))^\circ=A^{-T}(K-z)^\circ.
\]
Therefore
\[
|(TK-Tz)^\circ|
=
|\det A|^{-1}|(K-z)^\circ|.
\]
Since \(|TK|=|\det A||K|\), the product is unchanged. ∎

### Lemma 2

Let \(s(K)\) be the Santaló point of \(K\). If \(T(x)=Ax+b\) is an invertible affine map, then
\[
s(TK)=T s(K).
\]

### Proof

By Lemma 1, for every \(z\in\operatorname{int}K\),
\[
|TK|\,|(TK-Tz)^\circ|
=
|K|\,|(K-z)^\circ|.
\]
Hence \(z=s(K)\) gives a minimizer of the volume product for \(TK\). Conversely, if \(w\in\operatorname{int}TK\) is a minimizer for \(TK\), then \(T^{-1}w\) is a minimizer for \(K\). By uniqueness of the Santaló point, \(T^{-1}w=s(K)\), so \(w=T s(K)\). ∎

---

## 2. Part A: simplices attain the conjectured value

Let
\[
\Delta_n=
\left\{
x\in\mathbb R^n:
x_i\ge 0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\le 1
\right\}.
\]
This is the standard \(n\)-simplex. Its vertices are
\[
0,e_1,\dots,e_n.
\]

### Lemma 3

The Santaló point of \(\Delta_n\) is its centroid
\[
c=\frac1{n+1}(1,\dots,1).
\]

### Proof

First, \(c\in\operatorname{int}\Delta_n\), since \(c_i>0\) and \(\sum_i c_i=n/(n+1)<1\).

Let \(s=s(\Delta_n)\). Every permutation of the vertices \(0,e_1,\dots,e_n\) extends uniquely to an invertible affine map \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) with \(g(\Delta_n)=\Delta_n\). By Lemma 2,
\[
g(s)=s
\]
for every such \(g\).

Now show that the only point fixed by all vertex permutations is \(c\). Any point \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) can be written uniquely as an affine combination of the vertices:
\[
x=\lambda_0\cdot 0+\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i e_i
=
(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n),
\]
where
\[
\lambda_i\ge 0,\qquad \lambda_0+\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n=1.
\]
A permutation of vertices permutes the barycentric coordinates \(\lambda_0,\dots,\lambda_n\). If \(x\) is fixed by all permutations, then all \(\lambda_i\) are equal. Thus \(\lambda_i=1/(n+1)\) for every \(i\), so \(x=c\). Hence \(s=c\). ∎

We now compute the polar of \(\Delta_n-c\).

### Proposition 4

For every \(n\ge 1\),
\[
|(\Delta_n-c)^\circ|=\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{n!}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
P(\Delta_n)=|\Delta_n|\,|(\Delta_n-c)^\circ|
=
\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}.
\]

### Proof

We have
\[
|\Delta_n|=\frac1{n!}.
\]
For \(y\in\mathbb R^n\), set
\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.
\]
Since the maximum of the linear functional \(\langle y,\cdot\rangle\) over the simplex occurs at a vertex,
\[
\max_{x\in\Delta_n}\langle y,x\rangle
=
\max(0,y_1,\dots,y_n).
\]
Also
\[
\langle y,c\rangle=\frac{S}{n+1}.
\]
Therefore \(y\in(\Delta_n-c)^\circ\) iff
\[
\langle y,x-c\rangle\le 1
\quad\text{for all }x\in\Delta_n,
\]
equivalently
\[
\max(0,y_1,\dots,y_n)\le 1+\frac{S}{n+1}.
\]
This is equivalent to the two families of inequalities
\[
-S\le n+1
\]
and, for every \(i=1,\dots,n\),
\[
(n+1)y_i-S\le n+1.
\]
Thus
\[
(\Delta_n-c)^\circ
=
\left\{
y\in\mathbb R^n:
-S\le n+1,
\quad
(n+1)y_i-S\le n+1
\text{ for }i=1,\dots,n
\right\}.
\]

This polytope is bounded because \(c\in\operatorname{int}\Delta_n\), so \(0\in\operatorname{int}(\Delta_n-c)\), and therefore its polar is bounded.

We determine the vertices.

Let
\[
v_0=(n+1,\dots,n+1)
\]
and, for \(k=1,\dots,n\),
\[
v_k=-(n+1)e_k.
\]

At \(v_0\),
\[
S=n(n+1),
\]
so
\[
-S=-n(n+1)\le n+1,
\]
and for every \(i\),
\[
(n+1)y_i-S=(n+1)^2-n(n+1)=n+1.
\]
Thus the \(n\) inequalities \((n+1)y_i-S\le n+1\) are active at \(v_0\). Their gradients
\[
(n+1)e_i-\mathbf 1,\qquad i=1,\dots,n,
\]
are linearly independent: if
\[
\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i((n+1)e_i-\mathbf 1)=0,
\]
then for each \(j\),
\[
(n+1)\alpha_j-\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i=0.
\]
Hence all \(\alpha_j\) are equal, and then the equation forces \(\alpha_j=0\). Therefore \(v_0\) is a vertex.

Now fix \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\). At \(v_k\),
\[
S=-(n+1),
\]
so
\[
-S=n+1,
\]
and for \(i\ne k\),
\[
(n+1)y_i-S=(n+1)\cdot 0+(n+1)=n+1.
\]
Thus the inequality \(-S\le n+1\) and the \(n-1\) inequalities with \(i\ne k\) are active at \(v_k\). Their gradients are
\[
-\mathbf 1
\quad\text{and}\quad
(n+1)e_i-\mathbf 1\quad(i\ne k).
\]
We check independence. Suppose
\[
\alpha_0(-\mathbf 1)+\sum_{i\ne k}\alpha_i((n+1)e_i-\mathbf 1)=0.
\]
For \(j\ne k\), the \(j\)-th coordinate is
\[
-\alpha_0+(n+1)\alpha_j-\sum_{i\ne k}\alpha_i=0,
\]
while the \(k\)-th coordinate is
\[
-\alpha_0-\sum_{i\ne k}\alpha_i=0.
\]
Hence \(\alpha_0=-\sum_{i\ne k}\alpha_i\). Substituting into the \(j\ne k\) equation gives
\[
(n+1)\alpha_j=0,
\]
so \(\alpha_j=0\) for all \(j\ne k\). Then \(\alpha_0=0\). Therefore \(v_k\) is a vertex.

There are no other vertices. Indeed, a vertex of a bounded polytope in \(\mathbb R^n\) is specified by \(n\) linearly independent active constraints. If \(-S=n+1\) is not active, then all \(n\) constraints \((n+1)y_i-S=n+1\) must be active, giving \(v_0\). If \(-S=n+1\) is active, then \(n-1\) of the constraints \((n+1)y_i-S=n+1\) must be active. If the inactive index is \(k\), the active constraints force \(y_i=0\) for \(i\ne k\), and then \(S=-(n+1)\) forces \(y_k=-(n+1)\), giving \(v_k\). Hence
\[
(\Delta_n-c)^\circ
=
\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,v_1,\dots,v_n\}.
\]

It remains to compute the volume. The difference vectors are
\[
v_k-v_0=-(n+1)(e_k+\mathbf 1),
\qquad k=1,\dots,n.
\]
The matrix with columns \(e_k+\mathbf 1\) is
\[
I+\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T,
\]
where \(\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)^T\). Hence
\[
\det(I+\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T)=1+\mathbf 1^T\mathbf 1=n+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
|\det(v_1-v_0,\dots,v_n-v_0)|
=(n+1)^n(n+1)
=(n+1)^{n+1}.
\]
Thus the simplex volume is
\[
|(\Delta_n-c)^\circ|
=
\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{n!}.
\]
Using \(|\Delta_n|=1/n!\), we obtain
\[
P(\Delta_n)
=
\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}.
\]
∎

Every simplex is an affine image of \(\Delta_n\), so by Lemma 1 and Lemma 2, every simplex has the same volume product. This proves the following.

### Theorem 5

If \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a simplex, then
\[
P(K)=\frac{(n+1)^{n+1}}{(n!)^2}.
\]

This proves the “if” direction of the equality case in Part A. It does not prove the lower bound for non-simplicial bodies, nor the “only if” characterization.

---

## 3. Part B: cubes attain the conjectured symmetric value

Let
\[
K=[-1,1]^n.
\]
Then \(K=-K\) and \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\).

By Lemma 2 applied to the symmetry \(T(x)=-x\), the Santaló point of \(K\) is fixed by \(T\). Since the Santaló point is unique, it must be \(0\). Therefore the symmetric polar
\[
K^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le 1\text{ for all }x\in K\}
\]
is exactly the polar at the Santaló point.

Clearly
\[
|K|=2^n.
\]
For \(y\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\max_{x\in[-1,1]^n}\langle x,y\rangle
=
\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i|.
\]
Hence
\[
K^\circ
=
\left\{
y\in\mathbb R^n:
\sum_{i=1}^n |y_i|\le 1
\right\}.
\]
This is the standard \(\ell_1\)-unit ball.

The volume of the \(\ell_1\)-unit ball is
\[
\frac{2^n}{n!}.
\]
Indeed, the ball is the disjoint union of its intersections with the \(2^n\) orthants. In the orthant determined by signs \(\varepsilon_i\in\{\pm1\}\), the linear change of variables
\[
u_i=\varepsilon_i y_i
\]
has determinant \(\pm1\), and the set becomes
\[
\{u\in\mathbb R^n:u_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^n u_i\le 1\},
\]
which has volume \(1/n!\). Thus
\[
|K^\circ|=2^n\cdot \frac1{n!}=\frac{2^n}{n!}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|K|\,|K^\circ|
=
2^n\cdot \frac{2^n}{n!}
=
\frac{4^n}{n!}.
\]
This proves the following.

### Proposition 6

For the cube \(K=[-1,1]^n\),
\[
|K|\,|K^\circ|=\frac{4^n}{n!}.
\]

Thus the cube attains the conjectured symmetric Mahler lower bound. This does not prove the lower bound for an arbitrary centrally symmetric convex body, nor the full equality characterization.

---

The following parts of the stated problem are not resolved in this manuscript.

No counterexample is constructed, so the conjectures are neither proved nor disproved here.
